methodology.title: Calculation methodology
methodology.subtitle: Where the numbers come from and the formulas used across the platform.
methodology.zero: When the denominator is zero the KPI is undefined and shown as "—" (never 0 or infinity).
methodology.aggregation: Aggregated KPIs are calculated from summed totals (e.g. period CTR = total clicks ÷ total impressions), never by averaging averages. Monetary values use decimal.
methodology.calculatedText: CTR, CPC, CPM, CPL, CPA and ROAS are never stored: the server calculates them on every request.

src.Manual: Typed by a user in the metrics screen or through the budget spend registration.
src.CsvImport: Imported from a CSV file after preview, validation and confirmation.
src.Integration: Reserved for future integrations (Meta, Google Ads). No integration is active in this version.

rules.spend: Spend has a single source: metrics (CampaignMetrics.Spend). Budget actual spend is synchronized from them.
rules.budget: Registering spend on a budget adds the amount to the campaign-level metric of that day — it never creates a second entry.
rules.leads: Platform leads (metrics) and CRM leads are shown separately and never summed.
rules.conversions: Platform conversions (metrics) and CRM conversions are shown separately. In the CRM we distinguish overall conversions, unique converted leads and sales.
rules.dedup: Each conversion has a unique key per campaign (external ID, lead+type or event fingerprint): the same event is never counted twice.
rules.metricsUnique: There is at most one metrics row per campaign + ad + day; imports detect duplicates before saving.
rules.reach: Aggregated reach is the sum of daily reach and may contain the same people on different days.
rules.revenue: Attributed revenue (metrics) differs from CRM sales revenue and from agency revenue.
rules.comparison: In comparisons, highlights only consider campaigns with minimum volume (≥ 100 clicks, ≥ 7 days of data and spend), and ROAS is only highlighted when all have attributed revenue.

dashboard.title: 1. Meet the Dashboard
dashboard.text: This is where the key campaign numbers live: how much was invested, how many people saw and clicked the ads and how much came back in sales. Use the filters above to choose client, platform and period.

client.title: 2. Register a client
client.text: Everything starts with the client: the business that hired the agency. Click this button to register name, contact, industry and the monthly ad budget.

campaign.title: 3. Create a campaign
campaign.text: A campaign groups ads with the same goal, for example getting WhatsApp messages or selling a product. Choose client, platform, objective and period.

budget.title: 4. Set a budget
budget.text: The budget is the amount planned for ads. The system compares planned vs. actual spend and warns you when usage reaches 80%, 90% and 100%.

ad.title: 5. Create an ad
ad.text: The ad is what people see: headline, text, call-to-action button and destination link. You get a live preview while writing.

creative.title: 6. Add a creative
creative.text: Creatives are the images, videos and copy used in ads. Upload the files here and then link them to the same client's ads.

results.title: 7. Record the results
results.text: Enter each day's numbers (impressions, clicks, spend, leads, conversions) or import a CSV spreadsheet. KPIs are calculated automatically.

metrics.title: 8. Understand the metrics
metrics.text: Click the ⓘ icon next to any KPI to see what it means, how it is calculated and a practical example. Turn on Beginner Mode to see explanations on every screen.

lead.title: 9. Register a lead
lead.text: Leads are interested people who left their contact. In the pipeline, drag the card between columns as the conversation moves forward, up to the sale.

report.title: 10. Generate a report

help.inK2: How to do it in K2 Marketing

intro.title: Introduction to Digital Marketing
intro.summary: What it is and why small businesses use the internet to sell.
intro.what: Digital marketing is the set of actions that promote a business online: social media, search engines like Google, websites and messaging. The goal is to be found by the right people and turn interest into customers.
intro.why: With a small investment you can reach people in your area or with specific interests and measure exactly what worked — something hard to do with flyers or radio.
intro.example: A neighborhood bakery in Belo Horizonte promotes its Saturday breakfast on Instagram to residents within 3 km of the store and tracks how many orders arrive on WhatsApp.
intro.inK2: Register the client, create the campaigns and record the results. The Dashboard shows the performance of everything in one place.

campaign.title: What is a campaign?
campaign.summary: A set of ads with the same goal and period.
campaign.what: A campaign is a promotional action with a clear goal, a period and a budget. It contains the ads that will be shown.
campaign.why: Separating by campaign lets you know which action brought results. Mixing different goals makes the numbers confusing.
campaign.example: A clothing store in Recife creates a "Summer Collection" campaign to sell through its online store, and a separate campaign to gain followers.
campaign.inK2: In Campaigns › New campaign, choose client, platform, objective, dates and planned budget. The status (active, paused, completed) is managed here.

ad.title: What is an ad?
ad.summary: The piece people see: copy, image and button.
ad.what: An ad is the message shown to the audience: a headline, text, an image or video and an action button such as "Shop now" or "Send message".
ad.why: The ad is what catches attention and makes people click. Testing different versions helps you find the message that works best.
ad.example: A beauty salon tests two ads: one with a photo of a blowout result and another with a customer testimonial, and compares which one brings more bookings.
ad.inK2: In Ads, enter headline, text, button and link. The preview shows how the ad looks. You can duplicate and compare up to 4 ads.

creatives.title: What are creatives?
creatives.summary: Images, videos and copy used in ads.
creatives.what: Creatives are the visual and written materials of ads: product photos, short videos, banners, carousels and ready-made copy.
creatives.why: A good creative stands out among many posts. Keeping everything organized by client avoids rework.
creatives.example: A burger shop in Curitiba records a 15-second video of a burger being assembled and reuses the same image in several ads.
creatives.inK2: In the Creative library, upload each client's images and videos and then link them to ads.

paidTraffic.title: What is paid traffic?
paidTraffic.summary: Paying platforms to show your ads.
paidTraffic.what: Paid traffic is when you pay platforms such as Meta (Instagram and Facebook), Google or TikTok to show your ads to a chosen audience. The opposite is organic traffic, which comes from unpaid posts.
paidTraffic.why: It reaches new people quickly and lets you control how much to spend per day. Results appear while there is investment.
paidTraffic.example: A pet shop in Campinas spends R$ 20 a day on Instagram to promote its grooming service to dog owners in the neighborhood.
paidTraffic.inK2: The amount spent on each campaign is recorded in the metrics and compared with the planned budget.

budget.title: How does a budget work?
budget.summary: How much to plan and how to track spending.
budget.what: A budget is the amount planned for ads in a period. It can be daily (e.g. R$ 30 per day) or total (e.g. R$ 900 for the month).
budget.why: Tracking the budget prevents overspending and shows whether the money is bringing results.
budget.example: A dental clinic sets R$ 1,500 for the month. Halfway through it has already spent R$ 1,200 (80%) and decides to reduce the daily spend.
budget.inK2: In Budgets, set the planned amount and period. Actual spend is calculated from the metrics and you get alerts at 80%, 90% and 100%. Remember: it is the client's media investment, not agency revenue.

leads.title: What are leads?
leads.summary: Interested people who left their contact.
leads.what: A lead is a person who showed interest and left a contact: filled in a form, sent a WhatsApp message or called.
leads.why: A lead is not a customer yet. Following each lead up to the sale shows which campaigns bring genuinely interested people.
leads.example: A driving school gets 30 messages from an ad. Of those, 12 ask for a quote and 5 enroll.
leads.inK2: In Leads, register each contact and use the Kanban pipeline: drag from New to Contacted, Qualified and Converted (or Lost).

conversions.title: What are conversions?
conversions.summary: The most important action you want the customer to take.
conversions.what: A conversion is the action you defined as the goal: a purchase, a booking, a sign-up or a contact.
conversions.why: Conversions show whether the campaign generated business results, not just views and clicks.
conversions.example: For a beauty salon, the conversion is a confirmed booking. For an online store, it is a completed purchase.
conversions.inK2: Record conversions manually or by spreadsheet. The system avoids counting the same event twice and separates overall conversions, unique converted leads and sales.

results.title: How to interpret results?
results.summary: Look at the numbers together, not just one.
results.what: Interpreting results means reading the KPIs together: reach and clicks show attention; leads and conversions show interest and business; CPL, CPA and ROAS show cost and return.
results.why: A single number can be misleading. Many clicks with few sales, or a high ROAS with very few sales, call for caution.
results.example: Campaign A had an 8x ROAS but only 2 sales; campaign B had a 3x ROAS with 60 sales. B brought more customers and a more reliable result.
results.inK2: Use the Dashboard, the campaign detail and the Compare campaigns screen, which only highlights results when there is enough data.

report.title: How to create a report?
report.summary: Show the client what was done and what happened.
report.what: A report summarizes a period's results with numbers, charts and observations so the client understands the return on investment.
report.why: Clear reports build trust and help decide next steps: increase, keep or adjust the campaigns.
report.example: At the start of every month, the agency sends the clothing store a PDF with spend, sales, ROAS and the best-selling campaigns.
report.inK2: In Reports, choose client and period and export to PDF or CSV. The executive report already includes automatic observations.

spend.name: Ad spend
spend.short: How much was spent on ads.
spend.meaning: The amount spent on ads in the period.
spend.formula: Sum of the spend recorded in metrics (not calculated).
spend.example: The bakery spent R$ 500 on one week of ads.
spend.interpret: It is the client's media investment, not agency revenue. Always compare it with what it brought in leads, conversions and revenue.

impressions.name: Impressions
impressions.short: How many times the ad was shown.
impressions.meaning: The number of times the ad was displayed on people's screens. The same person may see the ad more than once.
impressions.formula: Value reported by the ad platform (not calculated).
impressions.example: The bakery's ad was shown 10,000 times on Instagram during the week.
impressions.interpret: It shows the size of the exposure. Many impressions with few clicks may mean the message or image did not catch attention.

reach.name: Reach
reach.short: How many different people saw it.
reach.meaning: The number of different people who saw the ad at least once.
reach.formula: Value reported by the platform. Adding up reach over several days may count the same person more than once.
reach.example: With 10,000 impressions and 6,500 reach, each person saw the ad about 1.5 times on average.
reach.interpret: Comparing reach with impressions shows frequency: if the same people see the ad many times, it may be time to refresh the creative.

clicks.name: Clicks
clicks.short: How many times the ad was clicked.
clicks.meaning: The number of times people clicked the ad to learn more, visit the website or open WhatsApp.
clicks.formula: Value reported by the platform (not calculated).
clicks.example: The ad got 400 clicks that led to the bakery's WhatsApp.
clicks.interpret: A click shows initial interest but is not a sale yet. Track how many clicks become leads and conversions.

ctr.name: CTR — Click-through rate
ctr.meaning: The percentage of ad impressions that generated clicks.
ctr.example: An ad had 1,000 impressions and 50 clicks. CTR = (50 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 5%.
ctr.interpret: This means that for every 100 impressions, about 5 generated a click. It is useful to compare ads in the same campaign and platform.

cpc.name: CPC — Cost per click
cpc.meaning: How much, on average, you paid for each click on the ad.
cpc.example: R$ 500 spent and 400 clicks: CPC = R$ 500 ÷ 400 = R$ 1.25.
cpc.interpret: It helps compare the cost of bringing people to the website or WhatsApp. A low CPC does not guarantee sales: also look at leads and conversions.

cpm.name: CPM — Cost per thousand impressions
cpm.meaning: How much it cost to show the ad one thousand times.
cpm.interpret: It shows the cost of reaching the audience. It varies with platform, chosen audience and time of year — dates like Black Friday are usually more competitive.

leads.name: Leads
leads.short: Interested people who left a contact.
leads.meaning: People who showed interest and left a contact: form, WhatsApp message or phone call.
leads.formula: Value reported by the platform or registered in K2's CRM (not calculated).
leads.example: 40 people messaged the bakery from the ad.
leads.interpret: Leads are opportunities, not sales yet. In K2, platform leads and CRM leads are shown separately so they are never counted twice.

cpl.name: CPL — Cost per lead
cpl.meaning: How much each lead cost on average.
cpl.example: R$ 500 spent and 40 leads: CPL = R$ 500 ÷ 40 = R$ 12.50.
cpl.interpret: Compare it with how much a customer usually spends. A higher CPL may be worth it if the leads are more qualified and buy more.

conversions.name: Conversions
conversions.meaning: The actions you defined as the goal: purchase, booking, sign-up or contact.
conversions.formula: Value reported by the platform or recorded in the CRM (not calculated).
conversions.interpret: What counts as a conversion depends on the campaign objective, so define it before you start. Always compare conversions of the same type.

cpa.name: CPA — Cost per acquisition
cpa.meaning: How much each conversion (sale, booking or sign-up) cost on average.
cpa.example: R$ 500 spent and 10 conversions: CPA = R$ 500 ÷ 10 = R$ 50.00.
cpa.interpret: Compare it with the profit of each sale or the value of a booking. If CPA is higher than the profit per sale, the campaign may be losing money.

revenue.name: Attributed revenue
revenue.meaning: The value of sales that the platform or the system attributed to the campaign.
revenue.example: The 10 orders added up to R$ 1,250 in sales.
revenue.interpret: It is the client's revenue, not profit and not agency revenue. The value depends on tracking rules (pixel, coupons, forms).

roas.name: ROAS — Return on ad spend
roas.short: How much came back for each R$ 1 spent.
roas.meaning: How much came back in sales for each real spent on ads.
roas.example: R$ 1,250 in sales with R$ 500 spent: ROAS = 1,250 ÷ 500 = 2.5x, that is, R$ 2.50 for every R$ 1.00.
roas.interpret: ROAS shows gross return, not profit: product costs still need to be deducted. A higher ROAS does not automatically mean the best campaign — also look at sales volume and objective.

simulator.title: Results Simulator
simulator.subtitle: Try different numbers and see the KPIs calculated instantly.
simulator.isolated: Isolated simulation: values stay on this screen only and do not change campaigns, metrics or financial data.
simulator.tip: Change one value at a time and watch the effect: for example, increase clicks while keeping spend the same and see CPC drop.
simulator.zeroNote: Nothing to divide by: the KPI is undefined (—).
simulator.warnClicks: Clicks greater than impressions: check the numbers (this does not happen with real data).
simulator.warnConversions: Conversions greater than clicks: possible but unusual. Check whether the conversions came from this campaign.

hints.spend: How much was spent on ads
hints.revenue: Value of sales linked to the campaign

examples.title: Example campaigns
examples.subtitle: Three small-business cases with the calculations explained.
examples.funnelNote: Each stage shows how many people moved forward compared with the previous stage.
examples.disclaimer: Fictitious results created for teaching only. They are not stored in the system and do not represent guaranteed results.

clickLeadSale.title: Click, lead and sale: what is the difference?
clickLeadSale.click: The person saw the ad and clicked to learn more. It is a sign of curiosity: 1,500 clicks.
clickLeadSale.lead: The person left name and phone asking about the lots. Now it is a real opportunity: 75 leads.
clickLeadSale.sale: After visits and negotiation, the lead closed the purchase. In real estate this can take weeks or months: 2 sales.

bakery.story: A neighborhood bakery promoted its Saturday breakfast delivery kit with Instagram and Facebook ads for nearby residents. The ad button opened a WhatsApp chat.
bakery.dataNote: Leads = WhatsApp chats started. Conversions = confirmed orders.

explain.ctr: 4% of impressions became clicks: for every 100 times the ad was shown, about 4 people clicked.
explain.cpc: Each person who opened WhatsApp cost R$ 1.25 on average.
explain.cpl: Each chat started cost R$ 12.50. If the kit costs R$ 125, a single order pays for several contacts.
explain.cpa: Each confirmed order cost R$ 50.00 in ads. The bakery should compare that with the profit of each kit.
explain.roas: R$ 1,250 in sales for R$ 500 spent: R$ 2.50 back for every R$ 1.00. This is gross revenue, not profit.

salon.story: A beauty salon advertised before-and-after photos of blowouts and coloring on Instagram, with a "Send message" button to book an appointment.
salon.dataNote: Leads = people who asked for an appointment. Conversions = appointments completed (average ticket R$ 90).

explain.ctr: 3% of impressions generated a click. Result photos usually spark interest in this industry.
explain.cpc: Each click cost R$ 1.25, the same as the bakery, but with a different audience and service.
explain.cpl: Each appointment request cost R$ 8.33: the ads brought low-cost contacts.
explain.cpa: Each booking cost R$ 16.67 in ads, well below the average service price (R$ 90).
explain.roas: R$ 1,620 in services for R$ 300 spent: a 5.4x ROAS. Half of the contacts booked, a sign of good lead quality.

realEstate.story: A real estate agency advertised lots in a new development on Facebook and Instagram, with a form for anyone who wanted the price list and to schedule a visit.
realEstate.dataNote: Leads = forms filled in. Conversions = lots sold (R$ 90,000 each) after visits and negotiation.

explain.ctr: 2.5% of impressions became clicks. Property is a big decision, so it is natural that fewer people click.
explain.cpc: Each click cost R$ 2.00 — more than in the other examples, because the audience is more specific.
explain.cpl: Each interested person cost R$ 40.00. It looks expensive, but each lead may be worth a high-value sale.
explain.cpa: Each sale cost R$ 1,500 in ads. Compared with the price of a lot, the cost is small.
explain.roas: A 60x ROAS looks huge, but it comes from only 2 high-value sales. With so few sales, one sale more or less changes the result a lot: evaluate it carefully.

glossary.title: Digital Marketing Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Terms explained simply, with an example and translation.
glossary.search: Search a term (in English or Portuguese)

campaign.name: Campaign
campaign.definition: A set of ads with the same goal, period and budget.
campaign.example: A stationery store's "Back to school" campaign, from Jan 15 to Feb 15.

ad.name: Ad
ad.definition: The piece shown to the audience, with headline, text, image or video and an action button.
ad.example: A photo of a cake with the text "Order for the weekend" and a "Send message" button.

creative.name: Creative
creative.definition: Visual or written material used in the ad: photo, video, banner, carousel or copy.
creative.example: A 15-second video showing a haircut being done.

paidTraffic.name: Paid traffic
paidTraffic.definition: Visits and contacts obtained with paid ads on the platforms.
paidTraffic.example: Spending R$ 20 a day on Instagram to promote a pizzeria.

impression.name: Impression
impression.definition: Each time the ad appears on someone's screen.
impression.example: If the same person saw the ad 3 times, that is 3 impressions.

reach.name: Reach
reach.definition: Number of different people who saw the ad.
reach.example: 3 people saw the ad 3 times each: 9 impressions and a reach of 3.

click.name: Click
click.definition: When someone taps or clicks the ad to learn more.
click.example: Tapping the "Learn more" button and opening the store's website.

ctr.name: CTR (click-through rate)
ctr.definition: Percentage of impressions that became clicks: (Clicks ÷ Impressions) × 100.

cpc.name: CPC (cost per click)
cpc.definition: Average amount paid per click: Spend ÷ Clicks.

cpm.name: CPM (cost per thousand impressions)
cpm.definition: Cost to show the ad one thousand times: (Spend ÷ Impressions) × 1,000.

cpl.name: CPL (cost per lead)
cpl.definition: Average amount paid per interested contact: Spend ÷ Leads.

cpa.name: CPA (cost per acquisition)
cpa.definition: Average amount paid per conversion: Spend ÷ Conversions.

roas.name: ROAS (return on ad spend)
roas.definition: How much came back in sales for each real spent: Revenue ÷ Spend.
roas.example: R$ 900 in sales with R$ 300 spent = 3x ROAS.

lead.name: Lead
lead.definition: An interested person who left a contact, such as name and phone.
lead.example: Someone who filled in the form asking for the party menu.

conversion.name: Conversion
conversion.definition: An important action taken by the customer, such as a purchase or a booking.
conversion.example: A customer booked an appointment through the ad link.

audience.name: Target audience
audience.definition: The group of people you want to reach, defined by location, age, interests or behavior.
audience.example: Women aged 25 to 45 within 5 km of the salon, interested in beauty.

remarketing.name: Remarketing
remarketing.definition: Showing ads to people who already interacted with the business, such as website visitors.
remarketing.example: Someone who added sneakers to the cart and did not buy later sees an ad for those sneakers.

funnel.name: Sales funnel
funnel.definition: The customer's path from discovering the business to buying: attention, interest, contact and sale.
funnel.example: 1,000 saw the ad, 50 clicked, 10 asked for a quote and 3 bought.

landingPage.name: Landing page
landingPage.definition: The page the ad takes people to, built for one specific action.
landingPage.example: A page with the course offer and a sign-up form.

pixel.name: Conversion pixel
pixel.definition: Code installed on the website that tells the platform when someone buys or signs up.
pixel.example: The pixel records the purchase and shows which ad led to the sale.

dailyBudget.name: Daily budget
dailyBudget.definition: The maximum amount the platform can spend per day on the campaign.
dailyBudget.example: R$ 25 per day for 30 days ≈ R$ 750 for the month.

tips.dashboard: This panel summarizes the campaigns in the selected period. Start with Ad spend and ROAS (how much came back for each R$ 1). Click the ⓘ next to any KPI to understand what it means.
tips.clients: Clients are the businesses served by the agency. Every campaign, ad, creative and lead belongs to a client.
tips.campaigns: A campaign groups ads with the same goal. The status here is internal to K2: pausing in the system does not pause the ad on the platform.
tips.budgets: Planned is what you intend to spend; actual is what has already been spent. The bar changes color at 80%, 90% and 100%.
tips.ads: Each ad belongs to a campaign. Select 2 to 4 ads to compare which message performed better.
tips.creatives: Store each client's images, videos and copy here. Then link them to ads.
tips.metrics: Each row is one day of results. Purple columns (CTR, CPC, ROAS) are calculated automatically from the entered values.
tips.leads: Leads are interested people. Drag the cards between columns as the conversation moves forward: New → Contacted → Qualified → Converted.
tips.conversions: Overall conversions count every event; unique leads count each person once; sales only consider purchases.
tips.campaignDetail: Track daily and per-ad performance. Compare spend with revenue to see whether the campaign is paying off.

charts.spend: Each bar shows how much was spent that day. Peaks may indicate budget increases or special dates.
charts.clicks: Shows how many times people clicked the ads each day.
charts.conversions: Compare the lines: leads are contacts; conversions are final actions such as purchases or bookings.
charts.roas: How much came back for each R$ 1 spent. Green: above 3x; orange: between 1x and 3x; red: below 1x (revenue did not cover the spend).
charts.platform: Compares spend and revenue on each platform (Meta, Google, TikTok...).
charts.budget: Shows how the planned budget is split across platforms.

reports.executive: A ready-to-present summary for the client: KPIs, comparison with the previous period and automatic observations.
reports.performance: Full table by client, campaign or platform. Use it to find where the investment performs best.
reports.budget: Compares what was planned with what was spent on each budget.
reports.leads: Shows how many leads arrived, where they came from and how many became customers.
reports.conversions: Shows conversions per day, type and campaign, including revenue.

campaign.intro: A campaign organizes ads with the same goal. About the fields:
campaign.name: A name that identifies the action, such as "Mother's Day Promotion".
campaign.objective: Choose the result you want to achieve, such as website visits, contacts or sales.
campaign.platform: Where the ads will run: Meta (Instagram and Facebook), Google, TikTok or LinkedIn.
campaign.budget: Amount planned to spend on ads during the campaign.
campaign.period: Start and end dates. Leave the end date empty for always-on campaigns.
campaign.audience: The group of people you want to reach. It is configured on the ad platform; describe it in the name or in the campaign tasks.

budget.intro: The budget defines how much to invest in media in a period.
budget.planned: Amount planned to spend on ads in the period.
budget.period: Date range of this budget. Periods of the same campaign cannot overlap.
budget.actual: Actual spend is calculated automatically from the recorded metrics.

spend.intro: Record how much was spent on a day. The amount is added to the campaign's spend for that day.
spend.amount: Amount spent on ads on the selected date.

ad.intro: The ad is what the audience sees. Write clearly and directly:
ad.headline: Short, catchy phrase, such as "Full breakfast for R$ 39".
ad.primaryText: Main text: explain the offer and the benefit in a few lines.
ad.cta: Action button: say what the person should do, such as "Send message" or "Shop now".
ad.url: Where the person goes after clicking: website, offer page or WhatsApp link.

lead.intro: A lead is an interested person who left a contact.
lead.source: Where the contact came from: form, WhatsApp, phone, referral...
lead.consent: Under the LGPD, record whether the person authorized contact.

conversion.intro: A conversion is an important action taken by the customer, such as a purchase or a booking.
conversion.type: Choose the type of action: purchase, booking, sign-up, contact...
conversion.revenue: Sale value, if any. Purchases must have a value greater than zero.
conversion.externalId: Order or transaction number. Prevents recording the same sale twice.

metric.intro: Enter the day's numbers as shown on the ad platform. KPIs are calculated automatically.
metric.impressions: How many times the ad was shown.
metric.reach: How many different people saw it (cannot exceed impressions).
metric.clicks: How many times it was clicked (cannot exceed impressions).
metric.leads: How many contacts the platform recorded.
metric.conversions: How many final actions (purchases, bookings) the platform recorded.
metric.revenue: Value of sales attributed to the campaign that day.

client.intro: Register the business served by the agency.
client.monthlyBudget: How much the client plans to spend on ads per month. It is not the amount paid to the agency.
client.industry: Line of business, such as "Food" or "Health". Helps compare results of similar businesses.
